lesson.title: Cutting the Continent: Building the Panama Canal
lesson.summary: The Panama Canal, completed in 1914 after a decade of construction and the defeat of deadly tropical disease, gave the United States Navy and merchant fleet a fast route between the Atlantic and Pacific and cemented American power in the Western Hemisphere.
lesson.body:
The idea of cutting a canal across the narrow isthmus of Panama to connect the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans had tempted engineers for decades, and a French company led by Ferdinand de Lesseps, the builder of the Suez Canal, made a major attempt in the 1880s. That effort collapsed, defeated by yellow fever, malaria, difficult terrain, and financial mismanagement, after thousands of workers died. The strategic case for finishing the job became much clearer during the Spanish-American War, when the battleship USS Oregon took more than two months to steam all the way around South America to join the fighting in the Caribbean, a delay that convinced naval planners the United States needed a shortcut between the oceans.

President Theodore Roosevelt made the canal a priority, and Panama was at the time a province of Colombia. When the Colombian senate rejected a proposed treaty in 1903 that would have granted the United States rights to build a canal, Roosevelt's administration supported a Panamanian independence movement, and when Panama declared independence in November 1903, the presence of American naval forces discouraged Colombia from suppressing the revolt by force. The new Panamanian government quickly signed the Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty, granting the United States control over a canal zone across the isthmus, an episode that critics at the time and since have viewed as a heavy-handed use of American power reminiscent of the interventionist habits the country had developed since the Spanish-American War.

Construction ran from 1904 to 1914 and required solving two enormous problems at once, engineering and disease. Colonel William Gorgas led an aggressive public health campaign against mosquitoes, applying lessons from Walter Reed's earlier research on yellow fever in Cuba, and dramatically reduced deaths among canal workers. Chief engineer John Frank Stevens redesigned the project around a system of locks rather than the sea-level canal the French had attempted, and Colonel George Washington Goethals took over as chief engineer in 1907 and oversaw the project through its completion. The canal officially opened in 1914, giving the United States Navy and world shipping a route between the oceans that saved thousands of miles of travel. The United States controlled the Canal Zone for decades afterward, a source of ongoing friction with Panama that was not resolved until treaties signed in 1977 set a timeline for transferring full control of the canal to Panama, which was completed in 1999.
